biography.plain_text: The Russian Orthodox Church, also known as the Moscow Patriarchate, is a multinational autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church. Its structure encompasses self-governing churches, exarchates, dioceses, parishes, monasteries, missions and theological schools. Its highest governing bodies are the Local Council, Bishops’ Council and Holy Synod, headed by the Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia.

long_biography.plain_text:
The Russian Orthodox Church traces its institutional history to the Christianisation of Rus' in 988. Its ecclesiastical centre moved from Kyiv to Vladimir and then Moscow, and it became effectively independent in 1448. The Moscow Patriarchate was established in 1589, formalising a patriarchal leadership recognised by the other Eastern patriarchs.

Its governing structure combines councils, the Holy Synod and a network of canonical units that includes dioceses, parishes, monasteries, theological institutions and missions. Alongside worship and pastoral care, its formal social teaching addresses charity, education, public morality, culture and cooperation with civic institutions. These functions are carried through church bodies rather than centred on any single officeholder.
